headline: The Tax Code's Open Secret: Legal Wealth Extraction at Scale
lede: The United States tax code does not merely tolerate certain wealth-preservation techniques used by the ultra-rich — in many cases, it created them. Understanding why these structures persist is less a story of villainy than of institutional inertia, lobbying arithmetic, and the durable American preference for taxing income you earn over wealth you inherit.
body:
The vocabulary of high-end tax planning is deliberately obscure, which suits its practitioners well. Terms like *grantor retained annuity trust*, *step-up in basis*, and *carried interest* occupy a bureaucratic register designed, consciously or not, to repel public scrutiny. But the underlying logic is straightforward enough: the U.S. tax code has, since its modern inception, treated returns to capital more favourably than returns to labour. A secretary paying income tax at 22 per cent on her salary occupies a different fiscal universe from a private equity partner paying 20 per cent on the same dollars, reclassified as long-term capital gains through a mechanism called *carried interest* — the manager's share of a fund's profits, taxed as investment income even though it represents compensation for services rendered.

The *buy, borrow, die* strategy is perhaps the most elegant expression of this asymmetry. A wealthy investor accumulates appreciating assets — equities, real estate, private company stakes — and holds them indefinitely, triggering no taxable event. When cash is needed for living expenses or new investments, the investor borrows against the portfolio, using it as collateral. Loans are not income; no tax is owed. At death, a provision in the tax code called *step-up in basis* resets the cost basis of the inherited assets to their fair-market value on the date of death, permanently extinguishing any capital-gains liability that had accrued over decades. The gain vanishes not through evasion but through expiration, written into statute. A 2021 report from the DC Fiscal Policy Institute estimated that the step-up provision costs the federal Treasury more than $40 billion annually in foregone revenues.

For those whose wealth is large enough to attract estate taxes, the *grantor retained annuity trust* — universally called a GRAT — provides another lever. The grantor places assets into an irrevocable trust, receives a stream of annuity payments back over a fixed term, and if the assets appreciate faster than an IRS benchmark interest rate (the so-called Section 7520 hurdle rate), the excess appreciation passes to heirs entirely free of gift and estate tax. In a low-rate environment, the hurdle is easily cleared. ProPublica, drawing on leaked IRS data, reported in 2021 that a single attorney who pioneered the GRAT technique estimated the structure had cost the Treasury roughly $100 billion over thirteen years. *Dynasty trusts* extend the logic across time: properly structured, they can hold family wealth in trust for centuries, insulating it from estate taxes at each generational transfer and, in states with permissive trust laws, from creditors and divorce proceedings as well.

Opportunity zones, created by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, illustrate how nominally public-benefit structures can be captured by private interests. Congress designated roughly 8,700 low-income census tracts as zones in which investors could defer or reduce capital-gains taxes by deploying proceeds into qualifying projects. The theory was economic revitalisation; the practice, as documented by ProPublica and academic researchers, included luxury hotels in already-gentrifying neighbourhoods, storage facilities, and golf resorts. *Captive insurance* companies offer a related arbitrage: a business creates its own insurance subsidiary, pays itself premiums that are deducted as business expenses, and parks the resulting reserves — often offshore — in low-tax jurisdictions. The IRS has listed certain captive arrangements on its annual list of abusive tax shelters, yet the structures persist in more carefully constructed variants.

The durability of all these arrangements reflects a political economy that is, at its core, self-reinforcing. The family offices — private investment vehicles that manage the affairs of the extremely wealthy, carved out of Dodd-Frank's disclosure requirements — employ attorneys, accountants, and lobbyists whose professional purpose is the perpetuation of the very rules they navigate. Every reform proposal — taxing unrealized gains above a threshold, treating carried interest as ordinary income, capping step-up in basis — runs into the same coalition of objectors: the financial-services industry, real estate associations, venture and private equity trade groups, and, more diffusely, the argument that taxing wealth destroys the incentive to create it. The Congressional Budget Office has scored closing the carried-interest preference as yielding roughly $14 billion over a decade — meaningful but not transformative — which makes it simultaneously a useful populist talking point and a structurally easy sacrifice to retain in exchange for other legislative priorities. It has survived every major tax reform of the past thirty years.

What makes this genuinely interesting to a systems thinker, as the original post suggests, is that it is not primarily a story about bad actors. The lawyers who design these structures are doing their jobs. The legislators who write the enabling statutes are often responding to legitimate constituent concerns about small-business succession and family-farm transfers, even if the ultimate beneficiaries are rather larger operations. The IRS enforces rules it did not write. The system produces outcomes that most observers find inequitable not because anyone intended inequality as a goal, but because a tax code assembled over a century, amended thousands of times, and lobbied at every joint, tends to stratify in the direction of whoever can afford the most sophisticated advisers. Reform, when it comes — if it comes — will have to reckon with the fact that the architecture is not broken. It is working exactly as its most recent renovators designed it.

concepts.definition: A wealth-preservation strategy in which an investor accumulates appreciating assets, borrows against them for living expenses (loans are not taxable income), and holds until death, at which point the step-up in basis eliminates any accumulated capital-gains liability for heirs.

The share of a private equity, hedge, or venture fund's profits paid to the fund's managers as performance compensation. Under current U.S. tax law, this fee — economically a payment for services — is taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rate (20%) rather than as ordinary income (up to 37%), provided the underlying investments are held for more than three years.

A provision in U.S. tax law (IRC §1014) that resets the cost basis of inherited assets to their fair-market value at the date of the original owner's death, permanently eliminating any capital-gains tax liability that had accrued during the decedent's lifetime.

An irrevocable trust in which the grantor transfers assets, receives fixed annuity payments back over a set term, and passes any appreciation above the IRS hurdle rate to heirs entirely free of gift and estate tax. Widely used by ultra-high-net-worth families to transfer large amounts of wealth with minimal tax cost.

A long-term (sometimes perpetual) trust structured to hold family wealth across multiple generations while minimising estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes at each inheritance. Permitted in states with favorable trust laws and designed to compound wealth outside the reach of estate taxation indefinitely.

A low-income census tract designated under the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act in which investors may defer or reduce capital-gains taxes by deploying proceeds into qualifying investments. Intended to spur economic development; critics note the benefits have often flowed to projects in already-appreciating areas.

A company-owned insurance subsidiary that insures the risks of its parent business. Premiums paid to the captive are deductible business expenses; reserves accumulate, often offshore, in low-tax jurisdictions. Legitimate versions exist; aggressive versions appear on the IRS list of abusive tax shelters.

fact_check: All structural descriptions (carried interest tax treatment, step-up in basis mechanics, GRAT hurdle-rate rules, opportunity zone legislation) reflect current U.S. tax law as of early 2026. The $40 billion annual cost of the step-up provision is sourced to the DC Fiscal Policy Institute (2021); the $100 billion GRAT figure is sourced to ProPublica's 2021 reporting on leaked IRS data, attributing the estimate to attorney Jonathan Blattmachr. The CBO's $14 billion carried-interest estimate is from the Congressional Budget Office's published budget options. The 20%/37% capital gains vs. ordinary income rate comparison reflects 2025 statutory rates. No facts have been invented.
